title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: ON THE ORIGIN AND USE OF MONEY.

Once the division of labour has been thoroughly established, the produce of a man's own labour can supply only a very small part of what he needs. He supplies by far the greater part of his wants by exchanging the surplus of his own labour's produce—whatever is left over beyond his own consumption—for the parts of other men's produce that he happens to need. Every man, then, lives by exchanging, or becomes to some degree a merchant, and the society itself grows into what is properly called a commercial society.

But when the division of labour first began, this power of exchanging must often have been badly clogged and hampered in its workings. Suppose one man has more of a certain commodity than he himself needs, while another has less. The first would naturally be glad to dispose of part of his surplus, and the second to buy it. But if this second man happens to have nothing the first one needs, no exchange can take place between them. The butcher has more meat in his shop than he can possibly eat, and the brewer and the baker would each be willing to buy some of it. But they have nothing to offer in exchange except the various products of their own trades, and the butcher is already supplied with all the bread and beer he immediately needs. In this case no exchange can be made between them. He cannot be their merchant, nor they his customers, and so they are all less useful to one another. To avoid the inconvenience of such situations, every prudent man in every period of society, after the division of labour was first established, must naturally have tried to manage his affairs so as to keep on hand at all times—besides the particular produce of his own work—a certain quantity of some one commodity or other that he imagined few people would refuse in exchange for the produce of their own labour. Many different commodities, it seems likely, were thought of and used for this purpose one after another. In the rough ages of society, cattle are said to have been the common instrument of commerce; and though they must have been a most inconvenient one, in old times things were frequently valued by the number of cattle given in exchange for them. Homer says that the armour of Diomede cost only nine oxen, but that of Glaucus cost a hundred oxen. Salt is said to be the common instrument of commerce and exchange in Abyssinia; a kind of shell in some parts of the coast of India; dried cod in Newfoundland; tobacco in Virginia; sugar in some of our West India colonies; hides or dressed leather in some other countries; and there is to this day a village in Scotland where, I am told, it is not uncommon for a workman to carry nails instead of money to the baker's shop or the alehouse.

In every country, however, men seem at last to have been driven by overwhelming reasons to prefer metals above every other commodity for this purpose. Metals can not only be kept with as little loss as any other commodity—scarcely anything being less perishable than they are—but they can also be divided, without any loss, into any number of parts, and those parts can easily be melted back together again. This is a quality that no other equally durable commodity possesses, and more than any other quality it makes metals fit to be the instruments of commerce and circulation. The man who wanted to buy salt, for example, and had nothing but cattle to give in exchange, would have been forced to buy salt to the value of a whole ox, or a whole sheep, at a time. He could rarely buy less than this, because what he had to give for it could rarely be divided without loss; and if he wished to buy more, then for the same reasons he would have been forced to buy double or triple the quantity—that is, the value of two or three oxen, or of two or three sheep. If, on the other hand, instead of sheep or oxen he had metals to give in exchange, he could easily match the quantity of metal to the precise quantity of the commodity he immediately needed.

Different nations have used different metals for this purpose. Iron was the common instrument of commerce among the ancient Spartans, copper among the ancient Romans, and gold and silver among all rich and commercial nations.

These metals seem originally to have been used for this purpose in rough bars, without any stamp or coinage. Thus Pliny tells us (Pliny, Natural History, book 33, chapter 3), on the authority of Timaeus, an ancient historian, that until the time of Servius Tullius the Romans had no coined money but used unstamped bars of copper to buy whatever they needed. These rough bars, then, served at that time as money.

The use of metals in this rough state involved two very considerable inconveniences: first, the trouble of weighing them, and second, the trouble of assaying them. With the precious metals, where a small difference in quantity makes a great difference in value, even weighing them with proper exactness requires at least very accurate weights and scales. Weighing gold in particular is a delicate operation; with the coarser metals, where a small error would be of little consequence, less accuracy would no doubt be needed. Yet we would find it excessively troublesome if, every time a poor man had occasion to buy or sell a farthing's worth of goods, he was obliged to weigh out the farthing. Assaying is still more difficult and still more tedious, and unless part of the metal is properly melted in the crucible with the right dissolving agents, any conclusion drawn from it is extremely uncertain. Before coined money was instituted, however, unless people went through this tedious and difficult operation, they were always liable to the grossest frauds and cheats; and instead of a pound weight of pure silver or pure copper they might receive, in exchange for their goods, an adulterated mixture of the coarsest and cheapest materials that had nevertheless been made to look like those metals on the surface. To prevent such abuses, to make exchanges easier, and thereby to encourage all sorts of industry and commerce, it has been found necessary, in all countries that have made any considerable progress toward improvement, to stamp a public mark on certain quantities of the particular metals commonly used in those countries to buy goods. This is the origin of coined money and of those public offices called mints—institutions of exactly the same nature as the aulnagers and stamp-masters of woollen and linen cloth. All of them are equally meant to certify, by means of a public stamp, the quantity and uniform quality of these different commodities when they are brought to market.

The first public stamps of this kind affixed to the metals in circulation seem in many cases to have been intended to certify what was both the hardest and the most important thing to certify—namely, the goodness or fineness of the metal. They seem to have resembled the sterling mark now stamped on silver plate and bars, or the Spanish mark sometimes stamped on ingots of gold, which, being struck on only one side of the piece and not covering the whole surface, certifies the fineness but not the weight of the metal. Abraham weighs out to Ephron the four hundred shekels of silver he had agreed to pay for the field of Machpelah. They are said, however, to be the merchant's current money, and yet they are received by weight, not by count, in just the same way that ingots of gold and bars of silver are at present. The revenues of the ancient Saxon kings of England are said to have been paid not in money but in kind—that is, in food and provisions of all sorts. William the Conqueror introduced the custom of paying them in money. This money, however, was for a long time received at the exchequer by weight, not by count.

The inconvenience and difficulty of weighing these metals exactly gave rise to the institution of coins, whose stamp, covering both sides of the piece entirely and sometimes the edges too, was supposed to certify not only the fineness but the weight of the metal. Such coins, therefore, were received by count, as they are now, without the trouble of weighing.

The names of these coins seem originally to have expressed the weight or quantity of metal they contained. In the time of Servius Tullius, who first coined money at Rome, the Roman as, or pondo, contained a Roman pound of good copper. It was divided, like our Troy pound, into twelve ounces, each of which contained a real ounce of good copper. The English pound sterling, in the time of Edward I, contained a pound, Tower weight, of silver of a known fineness. The Tower pound seems to have been somewhat more than the Roman pound and somewhat less than the Troy pound. The Troy pound was not introduced into the mint of England until the eighteenth year of Henry VIII. The French livre, in the time of Charlemagne, contained a pound, Troy weight, of silver of a known fineness. The fair of Troyes in Champagne was at that time attended by all the nations of Europe, and the weights and measures of so famous a market were generally known and respected. The Scots money pound, from the time of Alexander I to that of Robert Bruce, contained a pound of silver of the same weight and fineness as the English pound sterling. English, French, and Scots pennies, too, all originally contained a real pennyweight of silver—the twentieth part of an ounce, and the two-hundred-and-fortieth part of a pound. The shilling, too, seems originally to have been the name of a weight. “When wheat is at twelve shillings the quarter,” says an ancient statute of Henry III, “then the wastel bread of a farthing shall weigh eleven shillings and fourpence.” The proportion, however, between the shilling and either the penny on the one hand or the pound on the other does not seem to have been as constant and uniform as the proportion between the penny and the pound. During the first dynasty of the kings of France, the French sou, or shilling, appears on different occasions to have contained five, twelve, twenty, and forty pennies. Among the ancient Saxons a shilling appears at one time to have contained only five pennies, and it is not unlikely that it was as variable among them as among their neighbours, the ancient Franks. From the time of Charlemagne among the French, and from that of William the Conqueror among the English, the proportion between the pound, the shilling, and the penny seems to have been uniformly the same as it is now, though the value of each has changed greatly; for in every country in the world, I believe, the greed and injustice of princes and sovereign states, abusing the trust of their subjects, have gradually reduced the real quantity of metal originally contained in their coins. In the later ages of the republic, the Roman as was reduced to the twenty-fourth part of its original value, and instead of weighing a pound came to weigh only half an ounce. The English pound and penny at present contain only about a third, the Scots pound and penny about a thirty-sixth, and the French pound and penny about a sixty-sixth part of their original value. By means of these operations, the princes and sovereign states that carried them out were able, in appearance, to pay their debts and meet their obligations with a smaller quantity of silver than would otherwise have been required. It was, however, only in appearance, for their creditors were really cheated out of part of what was owed to them. All other debtors in the state were allowed the same privilege and could repay, with the same nominal sum in the new and debased coin, whatever they had borrowed in the old. Such operations, therefore, have always proved favourable to the debtor and ruinous to the creditor, and have sometimes produced a greater and more widespread revolution in the fortunes of private persons than could have been caused by a very great public disaster.
It is in this way that money has become, in all civilized nations, the universal instrument of commerce, through which goods of every kind are bought and sold, or exchanged for one another.

I shall now go on to examine what rules men naturally follow in exchanging goods either for money or for one another. These rules determine what may be called the relative, or exchangeable, value of goods.

The word VALUE, it should be noted, has two different meanings: sometimes it expresses the usefulness of a particular object, and sometimes the power of buying other goods that possession of that object brings. The first may be called “value in use”; the second, “value in exchange.” The things that have the greatest value in use frequently have little or no value in exchange; and, on the contrary, those that have the greatest value in exchange frequently have little or no value in use. Nothing is more useful than water, but it will buy scarcely anything; scarcely anything can be had in exchange for it. A diamond, on the contrary, has scarcely any value in use, yet a very great quantity of other goods can frequently be had in exchange for it.
In order to investigate the principles that govern the exchangeable value of commodities, I shall try to show:
First, what is the real measure of this exchangeable value; that is, what the real price of all commodities consists of.
Second, what are the different parts of which this real price is composed.

And, lastly, what are the different circumstances that sometimes raise some or all of these different parts of price above their natural or ordinary rate, and sometimes sink them below it; or, in other words, what are the causes that sometimes prevent the market price—that is, the actual price of commodities—from coinciding exactly with what may be called their natural price.

I shall try to explain these three subjects as fully and clearly as I can in the three following chapters, and for this I must very earnestly beg the reader for both patience and attention: his patience, to work through a detailed account that may in some places seem unnecessarily tedious; and his attention, to understand what may, even after the fullest explanation I am able to give, still appear somewhat obscure. I am always willing to risk being tedious in order to be sure I am clear; and even after taking the utmost pains to be clear, some obscurity may still remain on a subject that is by its very nature extremely abstract.
